newsitem.title: USA: ADM allowed to sell to government despite price-fixing.
newsitem.headline: ADM allowed to sell to government despite price-fixing.

text.p: The Agriculture Department Friday said agribusiness giant Archer Daniels Midland Co. could continue to do business with the government despite the company's recent guilty plea to price-fixing charges.

As a condition to continue selling its products to federal programmes, including school lunches and food aid abroad, ADM signed an agreement giving the department access to company records, ensuring that managers are warned against violating antitrust laws and setting company policies to follow the law.
The company said it would have "no comment whatsoever" on the decision.

ADM, whose slogan is "Supermarket to the World," is the nation's largest publicly traded grain processor. Headquartered in Decatur, Ill. its chairman, Dwayne Andreas, has long been one of the most politically influential figures in the agricultural industry.

The department said it had been investigating whether to bar ADM after the company agreed in October to plead guilty to two counts of price-fixing in food and feed additives and to pay a record $100 million in fines.

Firms convicted of breaking federal law can be barred from doing business with the government. The department recently barred the big California fruit concern, Sun Diamond, for three years because of its criminal convictions for giving illegal gifts to former Agriculture Secretary Mike Espy.
Grant Buntrock, a high level Agriculture Department manager, said ADM did not violate any department regulations.

"ADM approached us to determine what would be needed for ADM to demonstrate its present responsibility to continue doing business with the government and this agreement followed," Buntrock said in a statement.

The three-year agreement calls for ADM to establish an education and compliance programme that would set up a corporate code of conduct and an antitrust compliance guide to be distributed to marketing and sales employees.
The department also suspended three former ADM officials from government contracts pending the outcome of indictments.

They are Michael Andreas, the former executive vice president and son of Dwayne Andreas; Terrance Wilson, a former vice president who headed the corn-processing unit; and Mark Whitacre, a former vice president and the chief government informant in the antitrust probe of the company.
Earlier this week, a federal grand jury handed up a sweeping 45-count criminal indictment against Whitacre that accused him of stealing more than $9 million from ADM.
The agribusiness giant has said it does less than $67 million in federal business. It has annual sales topping $12 billion.
ADM products are used in the government's Food for Peace and Food for Progress programmes, which donate or aid food sales overseas, and in U.S. school lunch and food for the elderly programmes.

The company sells corn byproducts and corn/soybean blends to the government that are used as high nutrition products in feeding programmes overseas. It also sells soybean oil, sunflower oil, wheat flour and bulgar to the government, industry sources said.

Sun-Diamond officials said they would not comment specifically on the ADM ruling, but said they were hopeful the agency will reverse its decision to bar Sun-Diamond and its affiliates from doing business with the government.
